overview: The Russian Federation took shape as the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991 and continued the Soviet UN seat. A 1993 constitution laid out a federal state, but families faced inflation, lost earnings and strain on services during the transition. Wars in Chechnya harmed civilians. Russian engineers also helped launch the first module of the International Space Station. School languages, kitchens and bathrooms vary across this vast country. Russia continues; the imported map starts in 1994, and later Russian claims over Ukrainian land are not validated by its polygons.

periods.title: Soviet breakup and federation
periods.summary: The federation continued the Soviet UN seat in 1991 and adopted a new constitution in 1993. The imported 1994 map begins later.

periods.title: Market transition and Chechen war
periods.summary: Inflation and falling income disrupted households. War in Chechnya brought severe civilian harm.

periods.title: Crash, recovery and space partnership
periods.summary: The 1998 financial crisis shook the economy, then growth resumed. Russian-built Zarya started ISS assembly in orbit.

periods.title: Uneven growth and diverse homes
periods.summary: Economic recovery changed many lives, while health, housing and educational conditions differed by region and community.

periods.title: Territorial dispute and international response
periods.summary: Russia claimed Crimea, but the UN General Assembly reaffirmed Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and rejected recognition of that change.

periods.title: Invasion of Ukraine and continuing state
periods.summary: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The UN General Assembly demanded withdrawal; Russia continues as a state, while its map must not treat seized Ukrainian land as recognized Russian territory.

items.text: In December 1991 Russia told the UN that it would continue the Soviet Union’s seat, including its Security Council seat. This was a change in state structure, not the beginning of the peoples living across its lands. The map’s 1994 start is later still.

A new constitution was adopted in December 1993. It described a federation and individual rights. The constitutional text was later amended, including in 2020, so a card should not pretend every line stayed frozen since 1993.

Moving from Soviet planning toward markets brought rapid inflation, lower real earnings and rising poverty in the 1990s. A family could discover that money saved for school shoes bought less the next week. World Bank researchers also warned that poverty measurements from this transition were imperfect.
Russia’s 1998 debt and currency crisis shook jobs and savings; economic growth returned in the following years. Recovery was a real change, but national averages cannot describe every household.

The wars in Chechnya in the 1990s and around 2000 caused major civilian suffering. Human Rights Watch interviewed witnesses to attacks, killings and displacement. A border label saying “Russia” does not tell a Chechen child what safety meant at home.

Some Russian cities had communal apartments where each family occupied a room and neighbors shared the kitchen, bathroom and toilet. If another family was making dinner, privacy and cooking time became a social negotiation. This was one housing type, not every Russian home.

Rosstat’s census separates individual houses, separate apartments and communal apartments and asks about rooms and amenities. Its toilet questions distinguish an indoor flush toilet from other arrangements. “Has a bathroom” is not a useful answer unless one asks whose door it is behind.

The constitution protects children and families and promises health care through public institutions. During the 1990s transition, however, World Bank research found that health and education systems were under severe strain. A right on paper and an easy appointment at a clinic were different things.

Article 43 of the Russian constitution says “Каждый имеет право на образование,” meaning “Everyone has the right to education.” This short Cyrillic sample comes from a Russian legal text; the constitution also recognizes native-language use, and schools serve communities with many other languages.

Russia spans communities with different languages and school needs. UNESCO documents programs for Indigenous and minority languages, including regional efforts. A child learning in Siberia or Kalmykia need not have the same home language as a child in Moscow.

sections.title: A space station and borders that matter

items.text: Russian engineers built and launched Zarya in 1998, the first International Space Station module. It was funded by the United States, built in Moscow and launched on a Russian rocket. “Zarya” means “sunrise”: a good name for a spacecraft that spent sixteen days alone before its new neighbor arrived.

The station was a collaboration involving Russia, the United States, Japan, Canada and European countries. A machine over Earth shows that scientific achievements can have many passports and many teams.

In 2014 the UN General Assembly reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and called on states not to recognize Russia’s change of Crimea’s status. A map polygon or government claim cannot by itself make a disputed annexation internationally accepted.

Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The UN General Assembly demanded that Russia stop the invasion and withdraw. This is part of the Russian state’s recent history and of Ukrainian families’ lives; the cartographic display must not quietly treat occupied Ukrainian land as recognized Russian territory.

Russia continues as a state, while former Soviet republics are separate countries and many peoples within Russia have distinct languages and histories. The 1994 imported border start is a dataset limit, not a founding date or proof of later territorial claims.

ending.text: The Russian Federation continues after emerging from the Soviet breakup in 1991. The imported 1994 map start is later than that transition. The UN General Assembly did not recognize Russia’s 2014 change to Crimea’s status and demanded withdrawal after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine; map polygons cannot settle those territorial questions.
